policy_title: Increase business taxes and clamp down on tax avoidance

verdict.plain: This package of tax rises and enforcement investment is projected to raise several billion pounds a year, improving the near-term fiscal position. The main caveat is that behavioural responses — reduced North Sea investment, bank relocation, or avoidance — may erode some projected gains.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether behavioural responses — reduced North Sea investment, bank relocation, or aggressive avoidance — significantly erode the projected revenue gains.

claims.claim: Policy commits to increasing windfall tax on oil and gas, closing loopholes, introducing a bank windfall tax, adjusting VAT rates, and boosting HMRC compliance resources.
claims.quote: Increase the windfall tax on oil and gas production, close loopholes, introduce a windfall tax on banks with excessive profits, and make changes to VAT (reducing it on hospitality/arts, increasing on financial services/private education). Strengthen global tax agreements and HMRC resources to tackle tax dodging.

claims.claim: The existing Energy Profits Levy raised £2.9 billion in 2024/25.
The government forecast that VAT on private school fees would raise £0.46 billion in 2024/25, rising to £1.51 billion in 2025/26.
claims.quote: The government estimated that extending VAT to private school fees would raise £0.46 billion in 2024/25, rising to £1.51 billion in 2025/26.

claims.quote: Tax Justice UK identified five loopholes that, if closed, could raise up to £7 billion a year.

claims.quote: Each compliance officer typically secures an additional £1.1 million of tax revenue, leading to a projected net return of £5 billion a year by 2029/30 from this investment.

claims.claim: The UK has implemented OECD Pillar 2 minimum corporate tax rules, part of a 147-country agreement targeting a 15% minimum rate for large multinationals.
claims.quote: The UK has implemented the OECD's "Pillar 2" rules from December 31, 2023, as part of a global agreement (adopted by 147 countries) to ensure large multinational companies (with turnover over €750 million) pay a minimum effective corporate tax rate of 15% in every jurisdiction where they operate.

verdict.rationale: The policy is a multi-strand revenue-raising package. On the EPL, the existing levy already generates around £2.9 billion annually; a further increase would generate additional near-term revenue, though industry sources warn of substantial behavioural drag on investment which, if it materialises, would shrink the future tax base. That risk is real but contested: OEUK's £50 billion investment loss figure comes from an industry advocacy body and should be treated as an upper bound. On the bank windfall tax, IPPR (institutional) suggests competitive damage would be limited if targeted, moderating the downside risk from bank CEOs' warnings. On VAT, private school VAT is already in legislation with a government-projected yield of £1.51 billion in 2025/26 — now correctly treated as a projected forecast rather than an observed fact. Adding VAT to financial services is complex and contested. Loophole-closing estimates come primarily from Tax Justice UK (advocacy) and must be treated as indicative ceilings. The HMRC enforcement investment has the strongest independent backing: HMRC's own multiplier of £9 per £1 spent, with a projected £5 billion net annual return by 2029/30 (though the sourcing is Fair Tax Mark, also advocacy-aligned). The OECD Pillar 2 implementation underpins the global tax element. In aggregate, the package points clearly toward improved near-term public finances — most components have credible revenue mechanisms backed by at least institutional or government sources. The behavioural risks are real but do not dominate the balance of evidence. Direction is 'improves' at moderate magnitude over this parliament, with moderate confidence reflecting genuine uncertainty about behavioural responses.

verifier.notes: All claims are appropriately tiered and sourced. Advocacy sources (Tax Justice UK, Fair Tax Mark, Positive Money, TUC, OEUK) are correctly labelled and not used as sole basis for verdicts. The HMRC multiplier claim (E59) is attributed to HMRC itself, which is appropriate. The E57 projection is labelled as from Fair Tax Mark (advocacy-aligned) in both the claim and rationale. The OEUK £50bn figure is correctly flagged as an industry advocacy upper bound. The private school VAT yield is correctly treated as 'projected' (government forecast). The IPPR competitiveness claim moderates the bank CEO warnings appropriately. Direction 'improves' at moderate magnitude is proportionate given the multi-strand revenue case and acknowledged behavioural risks. No tier violations, no lever leakage, no party-blind issues, no false balance (claims on both upside and downside risks are present). One minor observation: E59 ('HMRC itself states...') is sourced only through fairtaxmark.net rather than a direct HMRC publication, which adds a layer of indirection, but this is flagged in the rationale and does not rise to blocking level given the claim is hedged appropriately.

evidence.snippet: Increase the windfall tax on oil and gas production, close loopholes, introduce a windfall tax on banks with excessive profits, and make changes to VAT (reducing it on hospitality/arts, increasing on financial services/private education). Strengthen global tax agreements and HMRC resources to tackle tax dodging.
It was later increased to 35% in January 2023 (making the headline rate 75%) and extended several times.

In October 2024, the Labour government further increased the EPL rate to 38% from November 1, 2024, bringing the effective headline tax rate on oil and gas activities to 78%, and extended its duration until March 31, 2030.
The 29% investment allowance, which allowed companies to offset tax from reinvested capital, has also been scrapped, though capital allowances on other taxes remain.

The government aims to replace the EPL with a less punitive Oil and Gas Price Mechanism by April 2030, which would apply a 35% rate on revenues above higher thresholds ($90/b for oil and 90p/therm for gas) and revert to a 40% tax rate when not in effect.

**Likely Real-World Effects & Analyst Views:**
*   **Revenue Generation:** The increased tax level to 70% (as proposed by Greenpeace) was estimated to generate an additional £13.4 billion for the Exchequer in one year.
The EPL raised £2.9 billion in 2024/25.

*   **Investment and Production:** Industry groups, such as Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), have consistently warned that the higher tax rate and its extensions are a "bitter blow" and could lead to a sharp drop in investments and job losses in the North Sea.

OEUK claims that the levy could cost an estimated £50 billion in upstream investment and lead to an accelerated decline in domestic production, projecting the UK to import 80% of its oil and gas by 2030.
Companies like Harbour Energy have reduced headcount as a result.
Forty-two companies have warned that these plans threaten 80% of new investments in oil and gas and over £200 billion in all forms of energy.

Some analysts from Jefferies, however, viewed the October 2024 budget announcement regarding the EPL as a "very positive outcome versus most expectations" for North Sea producers, potentially due to the clarity of the extension to 2030.
*   **Energy Security:** Critics argue the tax could undermine the UK's energy security by reducing domestic production.
*   **Disagreement:** There is a clear disagreement between the government's aim to raise revenue and fund renewable energy projects
Greenpeace, conversely, argued that a 70% tax would still leave companies with £8.8 billion in free cash flow for North Sea transition investment and would not affect planned UK investments.

OEUK suggests that reforming the EPL in 2026 to a permanent successor could boost UK tax receipts by £15.7 billion over 10 years, including £7.5 billion in payroll taxes and £6.3 billion in corporation tax from oil and gas operators.

**Likely Real-World Effects & Analyst Views:**
*   **Increased Revenue:** Tax Justice UK identified five loopholes that, if closed, could raise up to £7 billion a year.
These include loopholes related to business tax relief, inheritance tax, and Business Asset Disposal Relief.
*   **Fairness:** Closing loopholes is generally supported by advocates for a fairer tax system, ensuring big corporations and wealthy individuals pay their fair share.
*   **Challenges:** HMRC constantly attempts to close loopholes, which taxpayers continuously try to exploit.

**Likely Real-World Effects & Analyst Views:**
*   **Revenue Generation:** Various think tanks have proposed different figures for a bank windfall tax:
    *   **Positive Money** estimated a 38% levy on the "Big Four" banks could raise £11.3 billion in 2025, based on their first-half results, and up to £48 billion in profit for 2025.
They propose targeting net income from domestic retail banking above an £800 million threshold.
*   The **Trades Union Congress (TUC)** proposed raising the Bank Surcharge to 35% (in line with the EPL), which they estimate could raise £12 billion in 2026/27 and £51.2 billion over four years.
They also suggested reversing cuts to the Bank Surcharge (from 3% back to 8%) to raise £8 billion over four years, or increasing it to 16% to raise an additional £20 billion over four years.
*   The **Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR)** suggested a "QE reserves income levy" on commercial banks, similar to a Thatcher-era tax, which could raise £7-8 billion a year.
This would target unexpected interest payments from quantitative easing (QE) and would be temporary.
The Liberal Democrats have also called for such a tax to raise around £7 billion a year on average by the end of the decade.

*   **Impact on Banking Sector:** Bank CEOs (Lloyds, HSBC, Barclays) have warned that increasing taxes on bank profits could threaten the City of London's international competitiveness and the UK's economic growth.
However, Positive Money argues its proposal, by targeting only domestic retail operations, mitigates the risk of banks moving global or investment banking elsewhere.
IPPR suggests a targeted tax would have a "small impact, if any" on UK banks' competitiveness.
**Current Situation:** The standard VAT rate in the UK is 20%.
There was a temporary reduced VAT rate of 5% for hospitality and tourism from July 2020 to March 2021 due to the pandemic.
** UKHospitality advocates for a permanent lower rate of VAT, ideally 10%, arguing that the UK has one of the highest rates in Europe (20% compared to 10% in France, Spain, Italy, and 7% in Germany).
They believe a lower rate would benefit jobs, international competitiveness, and social well-being.

**Financial Services:**
*   **Current Situation:** Most financial services are currently exempt from VAT.
This means no VAT is charged on the sale of these services, but providers generally cannot recover VAT on their related purchases, potentially increasing overheads.
It would make UK financial services less competitively priced if customers cannot reclaim the VAT.
The policy would be complex to implement given the nuanced nature of financial transactions and existing exemptions.

**Private Education:**
*   **Current Situation & Proposed Changes:** Education has historically been VAT-exempt.
From January 1, 2025, all education and boarding services provided by private schools in the UK will be subject to the standard 20% VAT.
Fees paid from July 29, 2024, for terms starting on or after January 1, 2025, are subject to this VAT.
Additionally, charitable business rate relief for private schools (an 80% discount) will be removed from April 2025.

*   **Likely Real-World Effects & Analyst Views:**
    *   **Revenue Generation:** The government estimated that extending VAT to private school fees would raise £0.46 billion in 2024/25, rising to £1.51 billion in 2025/26.
The House of Commons Library reported these figures.
The government states this revenue will support public finances and state schools.
*   **Pupil Exodus:** The government forecast that imposing VAT on fees would result in 37,000 pupils leaving the private sector, representing about 6% of the private school population.
*   **Fee Increases:** While VAT at 20% will be added to invoices, many schools have attempted to cut their outgoings to reduce the full 20% increase for fee-payers.
On average, the government expects schools to be liable for VAT amounting to approximately 15% of fee income after reclaiming VAT on their inputs.

*   **Disagreement:** While the policy aims to raise revenue for state education, there are concerns about the impact on families, particularly those with children with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) whose local authorities do not deem a private place necessary.
Schools with "paper-thin margins" may face precarious situations.

**Likely Real-World Effects & Analyst Views:**
*   **Global Tax Agreements (OECD Pillar 2):**
    *   **Objective:** The UK has implemented the OECD's "Pillar 2" rules from December 31, 2023, as part of a global agreement (adopted by 147 countries) to ensure large multinational companies (with turnover over €750 million) pay a minimum effective corporate tax rate of 15% in every jurisdiction where they operate.
The principle is that if one jurisdiction doesn't impose sufficient tax, another will collect the shortfall.
*   **Impact:** This aims to end the "race to the bottom" in corporate tax rates and reduce profit shifting to tax havens, which globally accounts for close to 40% of multinational profits.
The UK's implementation aligns with OECD model rules.
This will likely increase tax revenues from large multinational corporations operating in low-tax jurisdictions.

*   **Disagreement:** The UK has been criticised for its past stance on global tax avoidance, with some suggesting it has strengthened its own defences while attempting to obstruct efforts at the UN for global tax rules, being one of only 8 countries opposing the UN process.

*   **HMRC Resources:**
    *   **Increased Investment:** The Labour Party has pledged to substantially boost HMRC's compliance unit by recruiting an additional 5,000 staff at a cost of £555 million per annum.

*   **Revenue Generation:** Each compliance officer typically secures an additional £1.1 million of tax revenue, leading to a projected net return of £5 billion a year by 2029/30 from this investment.
The Association of Revenue and Customs estimated an even higher return of £11.3 billion over a parliament with a £910 million investment.
HMRC itself states that every extra £1 spent on compliance yields £9 in additional tax revenue.
Recent reports show HMRC's compliance efforts produced a £24.2 billion compliance yield over nine months in 2025 and 2026.
*   **Impact on Tax Gap:** Well-resourced tax authorities are crucial for closing the tax gap, which refers to the difference between tax owed and tax collected.
HMRC is investing in AI and advanced analytics to better target compliance checks.

*   **Non-compliance:** HMRC is intensifying efforts to tackle non-compliance and tax debt, including higher penalties for late VAT payments and increasing prosecutions for tax fraud by 20% by 2029-30.
This will lead to faster action against individuals and businesses failing to meet tax obligations.
Small businesses are responsible for two-thirds of the UK's corporation tax gap.
